turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): right, before you go in, blood pressure's 128 over 76 and the pulse is 72. doctor's still stuck on the computer.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): sorry, say the blood pressure again? this screen's frozen.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): 128 over 76, pulse 72. she's brought her sister in with her.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. um, so what can I do for you?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): it's my heel, doctor. the first steps in the morning are really sore, like a nail. I've been panicking it's something awful.
[SEG0006] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): she's playing it down. it's been three months and she can barely put any weight on that heel, limping round the shop all day.
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): no, that's not fair. it's two months, not three, and I can put weight on it. I walk fine once I've got going. I even did parkrun on Sunday.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): uh, hang on, I've clicked the wrong bit. so somewhere between two and three months? which foot?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): the right heel. I'm saying two months. it came on after I got these new running shoes, the offer ones from work. I think I've overdone it, if I'm honest.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): new shoes. ok. what's it like through the day?

[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): first thing my feet feel dead, then the right heel stabs. by the end of the shift I feel like a wet rag. and the shop radio, honestly I can't hear myself think, but that's just the noise, not my hearing.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): sorry, an alert popped up. feet feel dead, both feet?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): yeah, both, just a minute or so, then it's the right heel. err, also I've had a frog in my throat for about a week. is that linked? I keep thinking it's something bad.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): a frog. say that again, I was typing.
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): throat's croaky, about a week. probably the dust in the stockroom. sorry, I fire questions when I'm nervous.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): you're alright. any swelling or redness on the heel?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): no. nothing like that. it looks normal to me.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): and does the pain wake you at night?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): no. once I'm asleep it's fine. it's the mornings.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): what about work, then? I can't read this note.

[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm a shop assistant in the sports shop on the high street, eight till six, five days a week, and some Saturdays. diet's a bit rubbish, sandwiches and crisps most days, though I do try a bit of salad. I run three times a week, about 5k. couple of glasses of wine at the weekend, no more than that, and I don't smoke.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): wine, sorry, how much? email just landed.
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Of. a couple of glasses, weekend only. that's it.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): any family illnesses, diabetes, blood pressure, hearts?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): um, my father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, my other sister has pressure but no sugar. my brother had his gallbladder out years ago but he's fine.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): medicines?

[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): I was taking ibuprophen, 400 milligrams three times a day, but I stopped it in March, it was burning my stomach. they gave me a script for naproxen and I never took it, packet's still in the drawer. now it's just paracetomol, two tablets, when the heel's really bad.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): stopped the ibuprofen in March, did you say? computer lagged.
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): yeah, March. haven't had it since. and I never started the naproxen.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): let me just feel. Mm. tender right under the heel, the plantar surface. no swelling that I can see. calf's a bit tight.
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): is it arthritis? am I going to need a scan, or an operation? should I give up running? and the throat, do I need antibiotics, and are the insoles dear?

[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): no, this sounds like plantar fasciitis, that first-step pain. no scan, no operation. calf stretches morning and evening, and get some gel insoles or a heel pad, they're not dear. keep running but ease off if it spikes, the throat isn't related so no antibiotics, and come back if it's not settling in six weeks.

spec.situation: Runner or shop worker with heel pain on the first steps in the morning for two months; new shoes mentioned; doctor suggests stretches and insoles; no tests.

traps.happens: In ONE long answer the patient lists several relatives and their conditions ('my father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, another sister has pressure but no sugar'), and in another long answer their job, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol.
traps.label_rule: Every relative with a stated condition is a separate family_history entry (relative, condition). Relatives said NOT to have a condition are not family_history entries. Occupation, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol/tobacco each become social_history entries as said (no inventions). Nothing from the doctor's questions is a fact.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: All details supported except duration; patient insists on two months, not 2 to 3 months.
bad.text: Right heel pain (category=musculoskeletal, status=present, duration=approximately 2 to 3 months, frequency=on first steps in the morning, onset=after new running shoes, temporality=current, body_site=right heel, aggravating_factors=first steps in the morning; new running shoes, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

omissions.text: Heel pain duration is specifically stated by the patient as two months, not 'approximately 2 to 3 months'.
Ibuprofen was stopped in March because it was burning her stomach.
Naproxen was prescribed but never taken; the packet is still in the drawer.
The patient denies hearing loss; she says the shop radio noise is the issue, not her hearing.
The heel looks normal to the patient.
Family history also includes mother without diabetes.
Family history also includes brother who had a gallbladder operation years ago.
The doctor advised no scan and no operation for the heel problem.
The doctor advised the throat symptom is not related to the heel problem.
